title: Indicators, dissemination and the way forward
text:
Who uses the accounts

Energy and climate policy: which industries drive demand and emissions, and where efficiency gains matter.
Economic planning: the energy and emission content of growth.
Modelling: input-output and general equilibrium models need energy and emissions by industry.
International reporting: SEEA, Eurostat and OECD formats, and comparison with other countries.

title: Indicators, dissemination and the way forward
text:
Reading the chart

Industries that use more energy per dinar also emit more per dinar.
Industries above the general pattern emit for reasons other than fuel: cement (process CO2), agriculture (methane), waste (landfills).
Both scales are logarithmic: the range between industries is very wide.

title: Indicators, dissemination and the way forward
text:
The place of households

Households used 34% of energy end use in 2022 (34% in 2015).
They emitted 11% of greenhouse gases in 2022 (10% in 2015).
Their emissions come from cars and homes; firewood, a large part of their energy, counts as biomass outside the CO2 total.

title: Indicators, dissemination and the way forward
text:
Dissemination formats

Tables: supply and use tables, accounts by activity and gas, bridge tables, indicators.
Workbooks in three languages, produced by the same code.
Documents whose text reads the data, and interactive charts on the web.
Open data: stable codes and separate label tables.

title: Indicators, dissemination and the way forward
text:
A dissemination calendar

Accounts for year t as soon as the balance, the inventory and the supply and use tables for t are available.
Revisions follow those of the sources; the pipeline recompiles the whole series in a minute.
Metadata and revision notes accompany each release.

title: Indicators, dissemination and the way forward
text:
What exists now

A complete first compilation of both accounts, 2015 to 2022.
An open pipeline that reproduces the IMF tools and runs in under a minute.
Documents, Excel products in three languages and a data explorer.
A list of assumptions and open questions, each recorded in a lookup table.

title: Air emissions accounts: sources and classifications
text:
What this presentation covers

What air emissions accounts are, and how they relate to the inventory.
The Tunisian inventory: gases, scope and files.
How inventory categories become industries and households.

title: Air emissions accounts: sources and classifications
text:
Why air emissions accounts?

The inventory classifies emissions by process: combustion in energy industries, road transport, enteric fermentation, landfills (Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, 2006).
It does not say which economic units emit.
The accounts reorganise the same emissions by industry and households, as in the national accounts (Eurostat, 2015).
Emissions can then sit beside output, value added, employment and the energy accounts.

title: Air emissions accounts: sources and classifications
text:
The Tunisian inventory

Coordinated by ANME (energy, industrial processes), the Ministry of Agriculture (agriculture, land use) and ONAS (waste) (Besbes, 2026).
IPCC 2006 guidelines, reported in the Common Reporting Tables (CRT) of the UNFCCC.
In 2022: 45.8 Mt CO2 eq excluding land use; land use is a net sink of -10.8 Mt.

title: Air emissions accounts: sources and classifications
text:
Scope of the accounts

Inside: CO2, CH4, N2O and fluorinated gases of energy, industrial processes, agriculture and waste.
Outside, in the bridge table: land use, land-use change and forestry (Eurostat, 2015, para 269).
Memo items: international bunkers (1.D) and CO2 from biomass (4.4 Mt in 2022), whose carbon was recently taken from the atmosphere.

title: Air emissions accounts: sources and classifications
text:
Preparing the inventory

CO2, CH4 and N2O come from Data, weighted by their warming potentials.
Fluorinated gases come from Summary2, where they are in CO2 equivalent by category.
Each category receives the most detailed code of the I2A tool to which it belongs.
The total including land use equals the net total of Summary2, once a small N2O difference is accounted for.

title: Air emissions accounts: sources and classifications
text:
Two classifications

Inventory: what process emits. Road transport.
Accounts: who emits. Households driving their cars, trucks of the food industry, buses of the transport industry.
Households appear as consumers: their cars and their homes. Households as producers, such as family farms, belong to their industry.

title: Air emissions accounts: sources and classifications
text:
The rule table

crt_to_activities.csv: a prefix of CRT codes, an activity and a reason.
Each category takes the longest matching prefix:

“3” covers all of agriculture;
“1.A.4.b” overrides “1.A.4” for homes.

A short table covers the whole inventory, and exceptions stay visible.

section: Keys shared with the energy accounts

Keys shared with the energy accounts

Road transport (1.A.3.b) is split between industries and households with the road key of the energy accounts.
Combustion in commerce and public services (1.A.4.a) is split among service industries with the tertiary key.
Both accounts therefore split these sectors the same way.

title: Energy accounts: classifications and allocation

What this presentation covers

The rows and columns of the energy accounts: products, flows and activities.
How each line of the balance finds its industry, and the two lines that need keys.
The concordance matrix, and what the converter does with it.

title: Energy accounts: classifications and allocation
section: Rows and columns of the accounts
text:
Rows and columns of the accounts

Rows: energy from natural inputs, energy products by group of the Standard International Energy Product Classification (SIEC), energy residuals (United Nations, 2018).
Columns: industries, households, accumulation, rest of the world, environment.
The IMF tool reports industries by ISIC section (A, B, C, D, E, F, H, other).
Tunisia uses the 24 industries of its supply and use tables, which add up to those sections.

title: Energy accounts: classifications and allocation
text:
Units

The balance is in thousand tonnes of oil equivalent (ktoe).
The accounts are in terajoules (TJ): 1 ktoe = 41.868 TJ (United Nations, 2018).
The IMF tool reports in petajoules (PJ): 1 PJ = 1,000 TJ.
The joule makes electricity, gas and oil additive by their energy content.

title: Energy accounts: classifications and allocation
text:
Two lines need keys

Road transport is given by mode, not by user: trucks, buses, taxis and private cars belong to many industries and to households.
Commerce, administration, hotels is one line for several service industries.
Both are split with keys from the supply and use tables of the same year:

road: purchases of refined petroleum products (product 19);
tertiary: purchases of electricity and gas (product 35).

title: Energy accounts: classifications and allocation
text:
Reading the keys

Households receive 34% of road fuel, transport 27%.
Refining and electricity are left out of the road key, since their purchases of product 19 are mostly transformation inputs.
Keys change every year with the national accounts.
They assume a similar price per unit of energy for every user: the best available information, but an assumption.

title: Energy accounts: classifications and allocation
text:
Default and Tunisian matrices

The default matrix of the tool allocates each flow to an ISIC section.
The Tunisian matrix replaces the rows of covered flows with one row per industry, with the factor of the key.
One matrix per year, because the keys change every year.
Imports, exports and stock changes keep the default rows.

title: Energy accounts: classifications and allocation
text:
What the converter does

Gives each flow its heading (supply, transformation, own use, final consumption).
Records primary production as a natural input from the environment, used by the extracting industry.
Multiplies each value of the balance by its factors.
Turns transformation outputs into supply of energy products.
Creates, for every use of energy, a residual of the same size returned to the environment.

title: Energy accounts: classifications and allocation
text:
Reading the diagram

Natural gas goes mostly into power plants, which turn it into electricity.
Oil products go to households, transport, manufacturing and agriculture; crude oil is also exported.
Biofuels, mainly firewood and charcoal, are used by households.
Transformation appears as a use of products; its output reappears as domestic production.

title: Energy accounts: classifications and allocation
text:
Points to discuss

Is the level of 24 industries right, or would finer detail be useful?
Electricity autoproducers and recovered heat: chemical industry?
Solar heat: produced and used by households? Non-energy use (bitumen): construction?
Could ONEM split the own use of the energy industries by industry?
Are money purchases a good enough key for road transport and services?

title: Energy and emissions accounts
text:
What this presentation covers

Why statistics on energy and emissions need accounts.
The System of Environmental-Economic Accounting (SEEA) and its energy and emissions accounts.
The three Tunisian sources that feed the accounts, and what each brings.

title: Energy and emissions accounts
section: Three systems describe the same economy
text:
Three systems describe the same economy

Energy statistics describe the supply and use of energy products on the national territory, by technical sector. In Tunisia, the national energy balance of ONEM.
Greenhouse gas inventories describe emissions on the territory, by process. In Tunisia, the inventory coordinated by ANME with the Ministry of Agriculture and ONAS.
National accounts describe the economy of resident units, by industry, in money. In Tunisia, the supply and use tables of the INS.

title: Energy and emissions accounts
text:
Each answers its own questions








System
Typical question
Unit of classification




Energy balance
How much natural gas was burnt in power plants?
Technical sector


Inventory
How much methane came from livestock?
Emitting process


National accounts
How much value did the food industry add?
Industry



None of them answers alone: how much energy does each dinar of value added require, and in which industry?

title: Energy and emissions accounts
text:
The questions policy asks

Which industries use the most energy, and the most energy per dinar of value added?
How much of household energy goes to transport, cooking or heating?
If the cement industry grows, how much do emissions rise?
Are energy use and emissions growing faster or slower than the economy?

These questions need energy and emissions organised like the national accounts.

title: Energy and emissions accounts
text:
The SEEA, an international standard

Adopted by the United Nations Statistical Commission in 2012 (United Nations et al., 2014).
A satellite of the System of National Accounts: same units, same classifications, same accounting rules.
Thematic guides for energy (United Nations, 2019) and air emissions; compilation manuals by Eurostat for both accounts (Eurostat, 2014; Eurostat, 2015).
Energy and air emissions accounts are among the SEEA accounts that countries compile most often.

title: Energy and emissions accounts
text:
Three kinds of energy flows

Energy from natural inputs flows from the environment into the economy: crude oil and gas when extracted, sun, wind, biomass.
Energy products circulate within the economy: produced, traded, transformed, used. Natural gas, diesel, electricity.
Energy residuals flow back to the environment: heat from burning fuels, electricity lost in the grid, gas flared at the well.

title: Energy and emissions accounts
text:
The flows in a picture






flowchart LR
  ENV1["Environment"] -- "natural inputs" --> IND["Resident industries"]
  ROW1["Rest of the world"] -- "imports" --> IND
  IND -- "energy products" --> IND
  IND -- "energy products" --> HH["Households"]
  IND -- "exports" --> ROW2["Rest of the world"]
  IND -- "residuals" --> ENV2["Environment"]
  HH -- "residuals" --> ENV2

title: Energy and emissions accounts
text:
Energy is conserved

Energy is neither created nor destroyed; it changes form (United Nations, 2019, paras 2.14 to 2.21).
A power plant burns gas: part becomes electricity (a product), the rest is lost as heat (a residual).
A household uses that electricity: its energy ends as residual heat too.
So every use of energy has a matching residual, and the totals of the tables exceed the energy actually consumed. This is a feature, not an error.

title: Energy and emissions accounts
text:
Territory and residence

The energy balance records what happens on the territory.
The accounts record what resident units do, wherever they are (Eurostat, 2014, paras 41 to 48).
A Tunisian airline refuelling in Paris: in the accounts, not in the balance.
A foreign ship refuelling in Radès: in the balance (bunkers), not in the accounts.
A bridge table reconciles the two totals.

title: Energy and emissions accounts
text:
Emissions in the SEEA

Emissions are residual flows into the atmosphere (United Nations et al., 2014).
Recorded for the economic unit that emits: industries, and households as consumers (Eurostat, 2015).
Same residence principle as the energy accounts, with a bridge to the inventory total.
Land use, land-use change and forestry stay outside the accounts and appear in the bridge.

title: Energy and emissions accounts
text:
The energy balance

45 flows and 23 products in 2022, in thousand tonnes of oil equivalent (1 ktoe = 41.868 TJ).
Supply (production, imports, exports, bunkers, stocks), transformation (power plants, refinery, charcoal kilns), own use, losses, final consumption by sector.
The layout changes between years: the pipeline reads labels, never cell positions, and stops on any unknown label.
Totals equal their parts to within 2.0 ktoe, the rounding of the published tables.

title: Energy and emissions accounts
text:
Production and imports









In 2022: 366 PJ of energy products from domestic production and 340 PJ from imports.

title: Energy and emissions accounts
text:
Reading the chart

Domestic production includes secondary products: electricity from power plants and products of the refinery.
Domestic production fell over the period while imports rose; imports exceeded domestic production in 2019.
Imports dipped in 2020, during the pandemic, and recovered in 2021.

title: Energy and emissions accounts
text:
The supply and use tables

24 products and as many industries, in millions of dinars at current prices.
They give the accounts their columns: the industries of the national accounts.
Their purchases of fuels and electricity provide the keys that split road transport and the tertiary sector.
Their output and value added turn energy and emissions into intensities.
Supply equals use for every product to within 0.08 million TND.

title: Energy and emissions accounts
text:
The greenhouse gas inventory

One CRT workbook a year; the Data sheet holds every reported value in long format.
Emissions by category, fuel and gas, and fuel use in terajoules.
In 2022: 45.8 Mt CO2 eq excluding land use, and a land-use sink of -10.8 Mt.
Data matches the published Summary2 for every category, with one small exception (N2O of 1.B.2.b.ii from 2019).

Points to discuss

Who maintains each file in each institution, and on what calendar?
Could the balance be shared in a stable layout, or with a code for each row and column?
The row « Fabrications métalliques » of 2015: iron and steel, or mechanical and electrical industries?
Is there a survey of fuel use by type of vehicle and user?

title: Documents
text:
Each document introduces the concepts it uses, explains the steps that the scripts carry out, and presents the results with figures and tables. Every number in the text is read from the tables published by the pipeline, so the documents follow the data each time the accounts are compiled again. Each document is also available as a PDF.




Physical energy flow accounts
How energy enters the Tunisian economy, which industries and households produce and use it, and how it returns to the environment. From the national energy balance to supply and use tables in terajoules, with indicators of energy intensity.
Read PDF






Air emissions accounts
Greenhouse gas emissions by industry and households. From the national inventory to accounts that follow the national accounts, with a bridge table and emission intensities.
Read PDF

title: Air Emissions Accounts for Tunisia
text:
Air emissions accounts (AEA) record the greenhouse gases emitted by each industry of the national accounts and by households, following the same rules as the national accounts. They answer a question that the greenhouse gas inventory, organised by technical process, does not answer directly: which parts of the economy produce the emissions, and how much they emit per dinar of output. This document explains the concepts, describes each step of a reproducible compilation of the accounts for 2015 to 2022, and presents the first results.
In 2022, resident industries and households emitted 46.9 million tonnes of CO2 equivalent. Carbon dioxide made up 71% of the total and methane 22%. The largest emitters were electricity and gas supply, non-metallic mineral products and agriculture, forestry and fishing, and households emitted 11% of the total, mostly from their cars and their homes. A bridge table reconciles the accounts with the national inventory, and the compilation reproduces the IMF Air Emissions Account Converter (I2A) to within 7e-12 kilotonnes.

title: Air Emissions Accounts for Tunisia
text:
2.1 Emissions as residual flows
The SEEA treats emissions as residual flows: substances released by economic activity that leave the economy and enter the environment (United Nations et al., 2014, Section 3.6). Air emissions accounts are the part of these accounts that concerns gases and particles released into the atmosphere. They follow the same accounting rules as the national accounts. Emissions are recorded for the economic units that generate them, namely industries, classified as in the national accounts, and households, in their role as consumers (Eurostat, 2015, paras 32 to 38). Emissions of households as producers, for example a family farm, belong to the industry concerned.

title: Air Emissions Accounts for Tunisia
section: 2.2 Greenhouse gases and their common unit
text:
2.2 Greenhouse gases and their common unit
The accounts cover the greenhouse gases of the inventory. Carbon dioxide (CO2) comes mainly from burning fossil fuels and from some industrial processes such as cement. Methane (CH4) comes from livestock, landfills and leaks of natural gas. Nitrous oxide (N2O) comes mainly from agricultural soils and manure. Fluorinated gases (HFCs, PFCs, SF6 and NF3) are industrial gases used in refrigeration, air conditioning and electrical equipment. Each gas warms the climate to a different degree, so emissions are converted into CO2 equivalent with global warming potentials over 100 years. Tunisia, like most countries, uses the values of the Fifth Assessment Report of the IPCC, in which one tonne of methane counts as 28 tonnes of CO2 and one tonne of nitrous oxide as 265 (Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, 2013).

title: Air Emissions Accounts for Tunisia
text:
2.3 Territory and residence
The inventory records emissions that occur on the national territory, whoever causes them. The accounts record emissions caused by resident units, wherever they occur (Eurostat, 2015, paras 33 to 37). A Tunisian airline flying from Paris to Montreal emits into the Tunisian accounts, while a foreign truck crossing Tunisia does not. The difference concerns mainly international transport. The accounts make it explicit in a bridge table, which starts from the total of the accounts, subtracts emissions of residents abroad, adds those of non-residents on the territory, and arrives at the total of the inventory (Eurostat, 2015, paras 227 to 230). Figure 1 shows how the two totals relate.







flowchart LR
  AEA["Accounts total<br/>(industries + households,<br/>residence principle)"] --> M1["minus residents abroad<br/>(air and sea transport)"]
  M1 --> P1["plus non-residents<br/>on the territory"]
  P1 --> INV["Inventory total<br/>excluding LULUCF<br/>(territory principle)"]
  INV --> L["plus land use, land-use<br/>change and forestry"]
  L --> NET["Inventory net total"]




Figure 1: From the air emissions accounts to the inventory total: the bridging items.

title: Air Emissions Accounts for Tunisia
text:
2.4 What the accounts leave out
Two items of the inventory stay outside the accounts. Emissions and removals from land use, land-use change and forestry (LULUCF) are not attributed to economic activity in the accounts and appear only in the bridge table (Eurostat, 2015, para 269). In Tunisia this sector is a net sink, with -10.8 million tonnes of CO2 equivalent in 2022, mostly from forests. Carbon dioxide from burning biomass, such as firewood, is a memo item in the inventory, since the carbon was recently taken from the atmosphere. It is kept apart in the accounts as well (4.4 million tonnes in 2022).

title: Air Emissions Accounts for Tunisia
text:
4.1 Preparing the inventory
The script 02_extract_crt_inventory.py stacks the Data sheets, removes exact duplicate rows, and compares the emissions added up by category with the totals of Summary2. They match for every category, gas and year, with one exception: nitrous oxide from category 1.B.2.b.ii, reported in Data from 2019 but not counted in Summary2, a difference of at most 0.24 kilotonnes of CO2 equivalent.
The script 20_prepare_ghg_inventory.py then builds a table of emissions by year, category and gas. CO2, CH4 and N2O come from Data and are weighted by their warming potentials. Fluorinated gases are reported in Data gas by gas but in CO2 equivalent only by industrial category in Summary2, so their totals come from Summary2. Each row is marked as part of the inventory total, LULUCF, or memo item. The inventory total, including LULUCF, equals the net total of Summary2 once the nitrous oxide above is taken into account.
The I2A tool knows a list of category codes that stops at the fifth level of the CRT classification, while the Tunisian Data sheet sometimes goes further, for example by animal sub-category. Each category therefore receives the most detailed code of the tool’s list to which it belongs.

title: Air Emissions Accounts for Tunisia
section: 4.2 From inventory categories to economic activities
text:
4.2 From inventory categories to economic activities
The conversion matrix gives, for each inventory category, the share of its emissions that goes to each economic activity. The I2A tool comes with a default matrix by ISIC section and households, which follows the correspondence of the Eurostat manual (Eurostat, 2015, para 12; International Monetary Fund, 2026). The script 21_build_conversion_matrix.py builds a Tunisian matrix by the 24 industries of the supply and use tables and households, from the lookup table crt_to_activities.csv. Each row of that table gives a prefix of CRT codes, an activity and a reason. A category takes the row with the longest prefix that matches its code, so that a short prefix (“3” for agriculture) covers a whole sector and a longer one overrides it for a sub-category.
Most categories belong to one activity: public electricity production to electricity and gas (35), cement production to building materials (23), enteric fermentation to agriculture (01), landfills to water and waste services (36). Two categories need keys, and they reuse those of the energy accounts, so that both accounts split these sectors in the same way. Road transport (1.A.3.b) is shared between industries and households in proportion to their purchases of refined petroleum products, and combustion in commerce and public services (1.A.4.a) is shared among service industries in proportion to their purchases of electricity and gas. In 2022, households receive 34% of road transport emissions.

title: Air Emissions Accounts for Tunisia
section: 4.3 Compiling the accounts and the residence adjustment
text:
4.3 Compiling the accounts and the residence adjustment
The script 22_compile_aea_tables.py applies the matrix to the inventory. As for the energy accounts, it does so twice: once by calling the function I2A of the tool unchanged, and once by applying each of its rules explicitly. The explicit version produces the accounts, and the script stops if the two differ by more than 10-9 kilotonnes. The rules are the following.

Inventory input. The inventory is laid out as the tool’s inventory sheet: one row per gas and category, one column per year, in kilotonnes of CO2 equivalent.
Allocation. Each value is multiplied by the factors of its category in the matrix. A category without factors receives nothing, which is why agricultural soils needed a Tunisian rule.
Air transport. The OECD estimates emissions of resident airlines on domestic flights and abroad (OECD, 2024). Where the OECD figure for domestic flights is lower than domestic aviation in the inventory, the difference is attributed to non-residents on the territory. Emissions of resident airlines abroad are added to air transport and recorded as a bridging item.
Maritime transport. Where the OECD estimate for resident vessels exceeds domestic navigation in the inventory, the difference is added to the activity.
Totals. The accounts total adds up industries and households, and the greenhouse gas total adds up the four gases.

Run with its default matrix, with and without OECD data, and with the Tunisian matrix for every year, the explicit version agrees with the tool to within 7e-12 kilotonnes (Table 4).

text:
4.4 Bridge table and checks
The script 23_bridge_and_indicators.py builds the bridge table of Table 5. Starting from the accounts total, it subtracts emissions of resident carriers abroad, adds those of non-residents on the territory, and must reach the inventory total excluding LULUCF. The gap is below 10-6 kilotonnes in every year and gas. Two features of the tool are worth noting, and the pipeline handles both. The positive gap of maritime transport is added to the activity without a matching bridging item, so the pipeline records it as residents abroad on water. And the tool’s own inventory total adds the bridging items without their sign; the bridge table uses the signed sum.

title: Air Emissions Accounts for Tunisia
text:
4.5 Indicators and export
Emission intensities divide emissions by output or value added at current prices, in tonnes of CO2 equivalent per million dinars. For households, the denominator is their final consumption expenditure, as the I2A manual suggests (International Monetary Fund, 2026). The script 24_export_aea.py writes the accounts to Excel workbooks in English, French and Arabic, with the long table, the bridge table, the accounts of each year by activity and gas, the emissions by source and activity, and the indicators.

title: Air Emissions Accounts for Tunisia
section: 5.1 Emissions over time and by gas
text:
5.1 Emissions over time and by gas
Figure 3 shows emissions of resident units by gas. They stayed close to 45 million tonnes of CO2 equivalent over the period, with a dip in 2020, when activity and travel fell during the COVID-19 pandemic.








Figure 3: Greenhouse gas emissions of resident units by gas (million tonnes CO2 eq).

title: Air Emissions Accounts for Tunisia
section: 5.2 From inventory sectors to the economy
text:
5.2 From inventory sectors to the economy
Figure 4 follows emissions of 2022 from the sectors of the inventory to the sections of the economy that emit them. Fuel combustion spreads over every part of the economy. Industrial processes come almost entirely from manufacturing, mainly cement. Agricultural emissions stay in agriculture, and waste emissions go to the water and waste industry. The residence adjustment adds the emissions of Tunisian carriers abroad to transport.




                            
                                            


Figure 4: Greenhouse gas emissions by inventory category and by section of the emitting activity, last year (kt CO2 eq). RES marks the residence adjustment.

title: Air Emissions Accounts for Tunisia
text:
5.3 Emissions by activity
Figure 5 ranks the emitters of 2022. Electricity and gas supply leads, followed by building materials, where cement kilns emit both from fuel and from the chemical transformation of limestone. Agriculture comes next, through livestock and soils, then households. Water and waste services owe their place to landfills.








Figure 5: Greenhouse gas emissions by activity and gas, last year (kt CO2 eq). The fifteen largest emitters.

title: Air Emissions Accounts for Tunisia
text:
5.4 Emission intensity
Across all industries, the economy emitted 326 tonnes of CO2 equivalent per million dinars of value added in 2022. Figure 6 shows how unevenly this is spread. A few industries, building materials, electricity, water and waste, and agriculture, emit far more per dinar than the rest. Policies that change the output of these industries, or the technology they use, have the largest effect on national emissions.

Data
The accounts use the national energy balances of the Observatoire national de l’énergie et des mines (ONEM), the national greenhouse gas inventory coordinated by the Agence nationale pour la maîtrise de l’énergie (ANME), and the supply and use tables of the Institut national de la statistique (INS). The residence adjustment of the emissions accounts uses estimates of air and maritime transport emissions by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD).

IMF tools
The compilation follows the PEFA Converter and the Air Emissions Account Converter (I2A) of the IMF Statistics Department, written by Achille Pegoue. The tools are published in the folder imf-tools/ of the repository with their manuals. The pipeline calls their functions unchanged to check its own explicit implementation.

title: Physical Energy Flow Accounts for Tunisia
text:
Physical energy flow accounts (PEFA) record, in terajoules, how energy enters the Tunisian economy, which industries and households produce and use it, and how it returns to the environment. They organise the information of the national energy balance in the format of the national accounts, so that energy use can be set beside output, value added and employment, and so that the emissions accounts can rest on the same allocation. This document explains the concepts, describes each step of a reproducible compilation of the accounts for 2015 to 2022, and presents the first results.
In 2022, the economy obtained 366 petajoules (PJ) of energy products from domestic production and 340 PJ from imports. Imports covered 62% of the natural gas supply. Households were the largest end user, with 34% of energy used for energy purposes, followed by transport and storage and non-metallic mineral products. Net domestic energy use, the accounts’ headline indicator, reached 494 PJ. The compilation reproduces the IMF PEFA Converter to within 5e-13 PJ, and every allocation choice is a table that the national compilers can review and change.

title: Physical Energy Flow Accounts for Tunisia
section: 2.1 Energy in the System of Environmental-Economic Accounting
text:
2.1 Energy in the System of Environmental-Economic Accounting
The SEEA follows energy as it crosses the boundary between the environment and the economy and as it moves within the economy. Three kinds of flows are distinguished (United Nations, 2019, paras 2.14 to 2.21). Energy from natural inputs flows from the environment into the economy, for example the energy content of crude oil when it is extracted, or the solar energy captured by a panel. Energy products circulate within the economy: they are produced, traded, transformed and used, for example natural gas, diesel or electricity. Energy residuals flow back to the environment: heat released when fuels are burnt, electricity lost in the grid, gas flared at the well head.
The accounts follow the principle of conservation of energy. Energy is neither created nor destroyed, only changed from one form to another. When natural gas is burnt in a power plant, part of its energy content becomes electricity, an energy product, and the rest is lost as heat, an energy residual. When a household uses the electricity, its energy content ends up as residual heat as well. For this reason every use of energy in the accounts is matched by a residual of the same size, and the totals of the supply and use tables are larger than the energy that the country actually consumes. Figure 1 shows these flows.







flowchart LR
  ENV1["Environment"] -- "natural inputs<br/>(crude oil, gas, sun, wind, biomass)" --> IND["Resident industries"]
  ROW1["Rest of the world"] -- "imports of<br/>energy products" --> IND
  IND -- "energy products" --> IND
  IND -- "energy products" --> HH["Households"]
  IND -- "exports" --> ROW2["Rest of the world"]
  IND -- "energy residuals<br/>(losses, heat)" --> ENV2["Environment"]
  HH -- "energy residuals" --> ENV2




Figure 1: Energy flows recorded in the physical energy flow accounts.

title: Physical Energy Flow Accounts for Tunisia
section: 2.2 Supply and use tables in physical units
text:
2.2 Supply and use tables in physical units
The accounts are presented as two tables with the same rows (United Nations et al., 2014, Section 3.3). The supply table shows who provides each flow: the environment provides natural inputs, industries produce energy products and residuals, the rest of the world provides imports, and households generate residuals. The use table shows who receives each flow: industries use natural inputs and energy products, households consume energy products, the rest of the world receives exports, and the environment receives the residuals. For each row, total supply equals total use. Columns are the same economic units as in the national accounts, namely industries, households, accumulation (changes in stocks and energy kept in products such as bitumen), the rest of the world and the environment.
The rows of the IMF tool follow the Standard International Energy Product Classification (SIEC) at the level of broad product groups: coal, natural gas, oil, biofuels, waste, electricity, heat and nuclear fuels (International Monetary Fund, 2024; United Nations, 2018). The columns of the tool follow the sections of the International Standard Industrial Classification (ISIC). The Tunisian accounts in this document go one level further and use the 24 industries of the Tunisian supply and use tables, which keeps them consistent with the national accounts and allows the results to be added up to ISIC sections when international comparison requires it.

title: Physical Energy Flow Accounts for Tunisia
text:
2.3 Territory and residence
An energy balance records what happens on the national territory. National accounts, and therefore energy accounts, record what resident units do, wherever they do it (Eurostat, 2014, paras 41 to 48). The difference matters mainly for international transport. Fuel that a Tunisian airline buys in Paris belongs to the Tunisian accounts but not to the Tunisian balance. Fuel that a foreign ship buys in Radès belongs to the balance as international bunkers, but not to the Tunisian accounts. The accounts reconcile the two views in a bridge table that starts from the accounts’ total and adds or subtracts these items to reach the total of the balance (Eurostat, 2014, paras 109 to 111).

title: Physical Energy Flow Accounts for Tunisia
text:
2.4 Units
Energy accounts are measured in joules. One terajoule (TJ) is 1012 joules, and one petajoule (PJ) is a thousand terajoules. The Tunisian balance is published in thousand tonnes of oil equivalent (ktoe). One tonne of oil equivalent is 41.868 gigajoules, so one ktoe equals 41.868 TJ (United Nations, 2018).

title: Physical Energy Flow Accounts for Tunisia
text:
4.1 Reading the energy balances
Because the layout of the balance changes over time, the extraction reads it by its labels, never by the position of its cells (see 01_extract_energy_balances.py in Annex I). The script finds the header row by its first cell, rebuilds product names from the two header rows, and puts the table in long format, with one row per year, flow and product. Each label of the source then receives a stable code from two lookup tables, one for flows and one for products. Some labels repeat, for example “Raffineries” appears among transformation inputs and among transformation outputs, so a flow is identified by its label and by the block of the balance in which it sits. The script stops on any label that the lookup tables do not know, which makes a change in next year’s workbook visible at once.
The published balances are rounded to the unit. Each total therefore differs slightly from the sum of its parts. The largest gap between a flow total and its components is 2.0 ktoe, and the largest gap in the identity that defines the energy available for final consumption is 1.5 ktoe, which confirms that the balance was read correctly.






NoteOpen question



The row « Fabrications métalliques » of 2015 could correspond either to iron and steel or to mechanical and electrical industries. It is read here as iron and steel, because the mechanical and electrical industries have no value before 2019. Both end up in the same industry of the supply and use tables (24), so the choice affects only the balance-level series.

title: Physical Energy Flow Accounts for Tunisia
section: 4.2 From the national balance to the IEA template
text:
4.2 From the national balance to the IEA template
The PEFA Converter reads a balance in the layout of the IEA: a fixed list of flows in a fixed order, a fixed list of products, values in terajoules and the IEA sign conventions, under which exports, bunkers, transformation inputs and own use are negative (Pegoue, 2026). The script 10_map_balance_to_iea_template.py moves each elementary cell of the Tunisian balance to its place in that template. Lookup tables give the default destination of each Tunisian flow and product, and a short list of exceptions handles cells whose treatment differs from the rest of their row or column (Table 3). Totals are not moved, since the tool recomputes them.

title: Physical Energy Flow Accounts for Tunisia
text:
4.3 Industries of the national accounts
The balance and the national accounts group users differently. For most flows the correspondence is direct: iron and steel and machinery belong to the mechanical and electrical industries (24), chemicals to the chemical industry (20), and so on. The script 11_build_activity_keys.py reads these rules from the lookup table balance_to_activities.csv, in which each row carries its reason. Two flows cannot be assigned to a single industry.

Road transport is given by mode, not by user. Trucks, buses, taxis and private cars all burn diesel and gasoline, and they belong to many industries and to households. The fuel is split in proportion to the purchases of refined petroleum products (SUT product 19) by each industry and by households in the supply and use tables of the same year. Refining and electricity are left out, since their purchases of product 19 are mainly transformation inputs.
Commerce, administration and hotels is one line of the balance for several service industries. It is split in proportion to their purchases of electricity and gas (SUT product 35).

These keys are an assumption. They rest on the idea that each user pays a similar price per unit of energy, which is not exactly true, but they use the best information available and change every year with the national accounts. Figure 3 shows them for 2022. Households receive 34% of road fuel.








Figure 3: Allocation keys for road transport and for the tertiary sector, share of each user, last year.











NoteOpen question



The road key mixes motor fuel with other uses of oil products, such as liquefied petroleum gas for cooking or fuel oil for heat. A survey of fuel use by type of vehicle and user, if one exists at the INS or at the Agence nationale pour la maîtrise de l’énergie (ANME), would give a more direct split.

title: Physical Energy Flow Accounts for Tunisia
text:
4.4 The concordance matrix
The concordance matrix is the heart of the PEFA Converter. For each flow and product of the balance, it says which PEFA product receives the energy, in which table (supply or use), for which activity, and with what share (International Monetary Fund, 2024). The tool comes with a default matrix that assigns each flow to an ISIC section. The script 12_build_concordance_matrix.py builds a Tunisian matrix for each year: it keeps the default rows for flows that the Tunisian rules do not cover, such as imports and exports, and replaces the rows of the covered flows by one row per industry with the factor of the key. The factors of each flow add up to one.
Most Tunisian rules fall within the ISIC section of the default matrix and only add detail. The rules for 6 flows move energy to another section (Table 4). Each move reflects a feature of the Tunisian economy or of the balance, and each is recorded with its reason.

4.4.1 International bunkers and residence
The balance records international marine bunkers, and its transport block includes the fuel delivered to aircraft on international flights. The script compares both with the memo items of the greenhouse gas inventory, which report the same fuel in terajoules. Aviation bunkers agree to within 0.45 percent in every year. Following the default matrix of the tool, bunkers are assigned to transport (49) as if all of them were bought by resident carriers.
The IMF tool can add residence adjustments in a sheet of bridging items: fuel bought abroad by resident carriers, and fuel bought in Tunisia by non-residents. The sheet is empty in the Tunisian run, since no source of these quantities is available yet.

The estimates of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) on air and maritime transport emissions, used in the emissions accounts, cover Tunisia and could serve as a first approximation.

title: Physical Energy Flow Accounts for Tunisia
section: 4.5 Compiling the supply and use tables
text:
4.5 Compiling the supply and use tables
The script 13_compile_pefa_tables.py applies the matrix to the balance. It does so in two ways. First, it calls the function EB2PEFA of the PEFA Converter itself, without changing it, by loading the tool’s Python code and passing it ranges built exactly as Excel would. Second, it applies every rule of that function explicitly, in readable code. The second version is the one that produces the accounts. The first serves as a reference, and the script stops if the two differ by more than 10-9 PJ in any cell.
The rules, in the order in which the tool applies them, are the following.

Levels of the flows. The tool reads the template from top to bottom and gives each flow the heading under which it sits: primary supply, transformation, own use of the energy industries, losses, and final consumption by industry, transport, other sectors and non-energy use.
Preparing the balance. The memo line for chemical non-energy use is subtracted from non-energy use in industry, to avoid counting it twice, and exports and stock changes change sign.
Preparing the matrix. Rows with a zero factor are dropped and the factors of each flow are normalised to add up to one.
Natural inputs. Primary production of an energy product is supplied by the extracting industry. The same energy is recorded as a natural input that the environment supplies and the industry uses. Renewable sources are a separate row from fossil resources.
Allocation. Each value of the balance is multiplied by the factors of its rows in the matrix and divided by a thousand, since the tool reports in petajoules.
Downstream flows and residuals. Transformation outputs become supply of energy products. Every use of energy in transformation, own use, losses, final consumption and bunkers creates an energy residual of the same size, supplied by the user and received by the environment. Non-energy use creates a residual that ends in accumulation, as energy stored in products.

On the tool’s own example, the two versions agree to within 5e-13 PJ. One feature of the example deserves mention. The example balance includes a “Total” column, and the default matrix has rows for that column on non-energy flows. When the column is passed to the tool, non-energy use is counted twice, and total supply (24,197.8 PJ) differs from total use (24,386.3 PJ). Without the column, both equal 24,009.4 PJ. The pipeline therefore passes the balance without its total column. On the Tunisian balance, with the default matrix and with the Tunisian matrix, for every year, the two versions agree to within 5e-13 PJ (Table 5).

title: Physical Energy Flow Accounts for Tunisia
text:
4.6 Checks and indicators
The script 14_check_pefa_and_indicators.py verifies three properties of the result.

Natural inputs and residuals balance exactly, since the tool creates both sides of each of these flows.
Energy products balance to within the rounding of the balance. The largest gap between supply and use of a product in any year is 3.3 ktoe, which comes from the rounding and the statistical difference of the published balance.
Energy use is plausible against money purchases. For each industry, the energy used is compared with its purchases of crude oil and gas, refined products, and electricity and gas in the supply and use tables. The ratio is an implied price in dinars per gigajoule (Figure 4). A user who buys energy without using any, or the reverse, would signal an error of allocation; no such case occurs.









Figure 4: Implied price of energy by industry: purchases of energy products in the supply and use tables divided by energy end use, last year (TND per GJ).





Refining (19) and electricity (35) are left out of the figure, because their purchases of energy products are mainly inputs to transformation, which the end-use figure excludes. The lowest prices appear in the miscellaneous industries, agriculture and building materials, which buy large quantities of heavy fuel, petroleum coke or natural gas at lower prices per unit of energy than diesel or electricity. Service industries show higher prices, because their energy is mostly electricity.
The script then derives the indicators of the accounts, following the Indicator sheet of the IMF tool and the key indicators of the Eurostat PEFA manual (Eurostat, 2014, para 101): use of natural inputs, production of energy products, transformation input, end use for energy and non-energy purposes, energy residuals, and net domestic energy use. This last indicator adds up the residuals supplied by each industry and by households and the energy kept in products used for non-energy purposes. It measures the energy actually used up by resident units, without the double counting of energy that is transformed before its end use (Eurostat, 2014, paras 103 to 106). Energy intensities relate end use to output and value added at current prices.

title: Physical Energy Flow Accounts for Tunisia
text:
4.7 Export
The script 15_export_pefa.py writes the accounts to three Excel workbooks, in English, French and Arabic, with the same numbers. Each holds a notes sheet, a long table of all years, the supply and use tables of each year in the layout of the PEFA sheet of the IMF tool, the same tables added up to ISIC sections, and the indicators. The workbooks can be downloaded from the Downloads page of this site.

title: Physical Energy Flow Accounts for Tunisia
text:
5.1 Supply of energy
Tunisia produces crude oil, natural gas, biomass and a growing amount of renewable electricity, and it imports a large share of its oil products and natural gas. Figure 5 shows that domestic production of energy products fell from 401 PJ in 2015 to 366 PJ in 2022, while imports rose from 317 PJ to 340 PJ. Domestic production here includes the output of power plants and of the refinery, which transform part of the primary energy.








Figure 5: Supply of energy products by origin (PJ). Domestic production includes secondary products such as electricity and refined products.

title: Physical Energy Flow Accounts for Tunisia
text:
5.2 From supply to use
Figure 6 follows each energy product from its origin to its use in 2022. Natural gas goes mostly into power plants, which turn it into electricity. Oil products go to households, transport, manufacturing and agriculture, and a large flow of crude oil is exported. Biofuels, mainly firewood and charcoal, are used by households. Stock changes are left out of the diagram, since a draw on stocks cannot be drawn as a flow.




                            
                                            


Figure 6: Energy products by origin and use, last year (PJ).

title: Physical Energy Flow Accounts for Tunisia
section: 5.3 Energy use by industry and households
text:
5.3 Energy use by industry and households
Figure 7 ranks the users of energy for energy purposes in 2022. Households lead, with 132 PJ, a share that combines cooking, heating, appliances and their share of road fuel. Transport and building materials (cement, ceramics, glass) follow with about the same amount each, ahead of agriculture and the miscellaneous industries.








Figure 7: End use of energy for energy purposes by user and product, last year (PJ). The twelve largest users.

title: Physical Energy Flow Accounts for Tunisia
text:
5.4 Energy intensity
Energy intensity relates the energy that an industry uses to the value it adds. Across all industries, the economy used 1.92 TJ per million dinars of value added in 2022. Figure 8 shows the wide range behind that average. Building materials use about 36 TJ per million dinars, several times more than transport or electricity, and service industries use much less. Because value added is measured at current prices, changes in intensity over time mix changes in efficiency with changes in prices.








Figure 8: Energy end use per million TND of value added, by industry, last year (TJ per million TND, current prices).

title: Physical Energy Flow Accounts for Tunisia
section: 5.5 Net domestic energy use and the energy balance
text:
5.5 Net domestic energy use and the energy balance
Net domestic energy use, the residence-based headline of the accounts, can be compared with gross inland consumption, the territory-based headline of the balance (Figure 9). In 2022 the first was 494 PJ and the second 487 PJ. Most of the difference comes from international bunkers (10 PJ in 2022), which the balance excludes from gross inland consumption and which the accounts, following the tool, attribute to resident carriers. A full bridge table between the two will require the residence data discussed in the methods.








Figure 9: Net domestic energy use of the accounts and gross inland consumption of the balance (PJ).

title: Physical Energy Flow Accounts for Tunisia
text:
01_extract_energy_balances.py
View on GitHub
This script reads the eight workbooks of the national energy balance as text, finds the header by the label “en 1000 tep”, rebuilds the product names from two header rows and puts each sheet in long format. Each row inherits the block of the last heading above it, so that labels which repeat can be told apart. Codes come from balance_flow_sources.csv and balance_product_sources.csv, and rows that receive the same code, as in 2015, are added up. Values are converted from ktoe to TJ. The script writes energy_balances.parquet and checks the hierarchies of flows and products and the identity of energy available for final consumption.

title: Physical Energy Flow Accounts for Tunisia
text:
02_extract_crt_inventory.py
View on GitHub
This script stacks the Data sheet of the eight CRT workbooks of the greenhouse gas inventory, which already hold every reported value in long format, adds the year, casts values to numbers and removes exact duplicate rows. It compares the emissions summed by category with sheet Summary2 and writes crt.parquet. The energy accounts use only its fuel use for international bunkers.

title: Physical Energy Flow Accounts for Tunisia
text:
03_extract_supply_use_tables.py
View on GitHub
This script reads one sheet per year of the supply and use tables. Column widths differ between periods, so blocks are found by the text of their headers, and the columns of the intermediate consumption matrix by their activity code. It writes sut.parquet in long format and checks that supply equals use for each product and that output equals intermediate consumption plus value added for each industry.

title: Physical Energy Flow Accounts for Tunisia
text:
10_map_balance_to_iea_template.py
View on GitHub
This script gives each elementary cell of the balance the flow and product of the IEA template read by the PEFA Converter, applies the exceptions of balance_template_exceptions.csv, and multiplies values by the IEA sign of their flow. It writes balance_iea.parquet and checks the conservation of energy and the IEA identity by product.

title: Physical Energy Flow Accounts for Tunisia
text:
11_build_activity_keys.py
View on GitHub
This script reads balance_to_activities.csv. Flows marked “direct” go in full to one activity. Flows marked “key” are split in proportion to the use of a SUT product by each listed activity in the same year. It writes activity_keys.parquet, with factors that add up to one for each flow.

title: Physical Energy Flow Accounts for Tunisia
text:
12_build_concordance_matrix.py
View on GitHub
This script reads the default concordance matrix of the PEFA Converter and replaces, year by year, the rows of the flows covered by the Tunisian keys. It writes concordance_matrix.parquet, the table of departures from the default ISIC sections, and a comparison of the bunkers of the balance with those of the inventory, and it confirms that the bridging items sheet of the tool is empty.

title: Physical Energy Flow Accounts for Tunisia
text:
13_compile_pefa_tables.py
View on GitHub
This script compiles the physical supply and use tables in two ways: by calling the function EB2PEFA of the PEFA Converter unchanged, and by applying each of its rules explicitly. It runs both on the example of the tool and on the Tunisian balance with the default and the Tunisian matrices, for every year, and stops if they differ by more than 10-9 PJ. It writes pefa.parquet (Tunisian matrix), pefa_isic.parquet (default matrix) and the agreement table.

title: Physical Energy Flow Accounts for Tunisia
text:
14_check_pefa_and_indicators.py
View on GitHub
This script checks that natural inputs and residuals balance exactly and that energy products balance to within the rounding of the published balance, compares energy use with purchases of energy products in the supply and use tables, and computes the indicators by activity. It writes the tables of balances by category and product, the plausibility table and the indicators.

title: Physical Energy Flow Accounts for Tunisia
text:
15_export_pefa.py
View on GitHub
This script writes pefa-accounts-en.xlsx, pefa-accounts-fr.xlsx and pefa-accounts-ar.xlsx in English, French and Arabic, with labels from the lookup tables. Arabic workbooks read from right to left.

title: Physical Energy Flow Accounts for Tunisia
text:
30_publish_tables.py
View on GitHub
This script publishes the tables and labels read by this document, the presentations and the data explorer in data/outputs/tables/ and data/outputs/labels/, in Parquet and CSV. It also derives the flow tables of the Sankey diagrams and gathers the checks of all scripts.

title: Energy and air emissions accounts for Tunisia
text:
This site presents the physical energy flow accounts and the air emissions accounts of Tunisia. Both follow the System of Environmental-Economic Accounting (SEEA) of the United Nations, which extends the national accounts to the environment. The accounts record, in terajoules and in tonnes of CO2 equivalent, how much energy each industry and households use and how much greenhouse gas they emit, with the same classifications as the supply and use tables of the national accounts.
The accounts are compiled by an open, reproducible pipeline of Python scripts. It reads the national energy balance, the greenhouse gas inventory and the supply and use tables, applies the logic of the IMF PEFA Converter and Air Emissions Account Converter, checks every step, and writes the accounts to Excel in English, French and Arabic. Every allocation choice is a table that compilers can review and change.




Documents
Concepts, compilation methods and results of the energy accounts and the air emissions accounts, with an annex describing each script.
Read the documents

Seven presentations, from the SEEA framework and the sources to the energy accounts, the emissions accounts and their dissemination.

title: The IMF tools and a reproducible pipeline
text:
What this presentation covers

The two IMF tools: what they take in, what they do, what they give back.
Why the same logic was rewritten as an open, reproducible pipeline.
How the pipeline is organised, how it checks itself, and how to run it.

title: The IMF tools and a reproducible pipeline
text:
Why tools?

Compiling accounts from a balance and an inventory means hundreds of correspondence decisions.
A tool fixes the sequence of steps and applies the international recommendations the same way in every country.
The IMF Statistics Department developed two Excel tools with Python functions, written by Achille Pegoue (Pegoue, 2026b, 2026a).

title: The IMF tools and a reproducible pipeline
The IMF tools and a reproducible pipeline
The IMF tools and a reproducible pipeline
text:
How the tools work






flowchart LR
  EB["Energy balance<br/>(IEA layout, TJ)"] --> CM{{"Concordance matrix<br/>flow × product → activity"}}
  CM --> PSUT["Supply and use<br/>tables (PJ)"]
  INV["Inventory<br/>(CRT, kt CO2 eq)"] --> CVM{{"Conversion matrix<br/>category → activity"}}
  OECD["OECD transport<br/>emissions"] --> CVM
  CVM --> AEA["Accounts and<br/>bridge table"]

title: The IMF tools and a reproducible pipeline
text:
Why rewrite the logic?

A workbook hides decisions in cells; a lookup table with a reason per row shows them.
Each year needs the same steps again: a pipeline repeats them in under a minute.
Checks run every time, and a failed check stops the run.
The same code writes the accounts in English, French and Arabic.
Anyone can read, rerun and challenge every number.

title: The IMF tools and a reproducible pipeline
text:
Two layers that must agree

Explicit layer: every rule of the tools rewritten step by step in readable Python. This produces the accounts.
Reference layer: the original tool functions, called unchanged, on the same inputs.
The run stops if the two differ:

energy accounts: largest gap 5e-13 PJ, all years and matrices;
emissions accounts: largest gap 7e-12 kt CO2 eq.

text:
What this presentation covers

Territory, residence and the bridge between the accounts and the balance.
The checks that every compilation must pass.
First results for 2015 to 2022, and how to disseminate them.

title: Energy accounts: residence, checks and results
text:
Territory and residence

The energy balance records what happens on the territory; the accounts record what resident units do, wherever they are (Eurostat, 2014, paras 41 to 48).
The difference is mostly international transport:

fuel bought abroad by Tunisian airlines and shipping companies belongs to the accounts;
fuel bought in Tunisia by foreign carriers belongs to the balance, not to the accounts.

Road transport can also cross borders: foreign trucks, cross-border purchases.

section: Net domestic energy use and gross inland consumption
text:
Net domestic energy use and gross inland consumption









In 2022: 494 PJ against 487 PJ.

title: Energy accounts: residence, checks and results
text:
Why the two differ

Net domestic energy use adds up the residuals of residents plus energy kept in products such as bitumen (Eurostat, 2014, paras 103 to 106).
Gross inland consumption excludes international bunkers (10 PJ in 2022).
Until residence data exist, the accounts attribute bunkers to resident carriers, as the tool does by default.
A complete bridge needs fuel bought abroad by residents and fuel bought in Tunisia by non-residents.

title: Energy accounts: residence, checks and results
text:
Three kinds of checks

Identities: supply equals use, row by row.
Agreement with the tools: the explicit layer reproduces the IMF functions.
Plausibility: the physical accounts make sense against the money accounts.

title: Energy accounts: residence, checks and results
text:
Supply equals use

Natural inputs and residuals balance exactly, since the converter writes both sides of each flow.
Energy products balance to within 3.3 ktoe, the rounding and statistical difference of the published balance.
The explicit layer matches the tool to within 5e-13 PJ.

title: Energy accounts: residence, checks and results
text:
Plausibility: implied prices

For each industry, divide its purchases of energy in the supply and use tables (crude oil and gas, refined products, electricity and gas) by its energy use in the accounts.
The result is an implied price in dinars per gigajoule.
An industry that buys energy but uses none, or the reverse, would reveal an allocation error. None appears.

title: Energy accounts: residence, checks and results
text: Implied prices in 2022

title: Energy accounts: residence, checks and results
text:
Reading the prices

Lowest prices: miscellaneous industries, agriculture, building materials, which buy heavy fuel, petroleum coke or gas, cheap per unit of energy.
Highest prices: services, whose energy is mostly electricity.
Refining and electricity are left out: their purchases are mainly transformation inputs.

title: Energy accounts: residence, checks and results
text:
Key figures for 2022

Net domestic energy use: 494 PJ.
Households: 34% of energy end use.
Energy intensity of the economy: 2.05 TJ per million TND of value added.

Next come transport and storage and non-metallic mineral products.
Oil dominates final use; natural gas matters for industry; biofuels for households.

Energy intensity

Energy intensity relates the energy an industry uses to the value it adds.
It shows where energy is concentrated in production, and where efficiency policies matter most.
At current prices, changes mix efficiency with prices: use with care over time.

title: Air emissions accounts: allocation, residence and results
text:
Default and Tunisian matrices

The I2A tool comes with a default matrix from inventory categories to ISIC sections and households, following the Eurostat correspondence (Eurostat, 2015; International Monetary Fund, 2026).
The Tunisian matrix uses the 24 industries and households, one matrix per year.
Each category’s emissions are multiplied by its factors; a category with no factors receives nothing.

title: Air emissions accounts: allocation, residence and results
section: A gap in the default matrix
text:
A gap in the default matrix

The default matrix has no factors for agricultural soils (3.D).
Without a Tunisian rule, 1,482 kt CO2 eq would disappear in 2022, silently.
The Tunisian matrix assigns them to agriculture.
The pipeline lists every category that the default matrix would drop.

title: Air emissions accounts: allocation, residence and results
text:
Three groups of changes

Road transport and residential combustion move from transport and construction to households, as the accounts require.
Natural gas transmission and distribution move from transport to electricity and gas, which runs the network.
Commercial refrigeration gases go to trade.

title: Air emissions accounts: allocation, residence and results
section: How the tool adjusts for residence
text:
How the tool adjusts for residence

Air: OECD estimates emissions of Tunisian airlines on domestic flights and abroad (OECD, 2024).
Emissions of resident airlines abroad are added to air transport and recorded as a bridging item.
If the OECD estimate for domestic flights is below the inventory, the difference goes to non-residents on the territory.
Sea: if the OECD estimate for resident vessels exceeds domestic navigation, the difference is added to water transport.

title: Air emissions accounts: allocation, residence and results
text:
Reading the bridge table

Start from the accounts total (residents, wherever they emit).
Subtract residents abroad; add non-residents on the territory.
The result equals the inventory total without land use, to within 10-6 kt, every year and gas.
Adding land use gives the net inventory total.

title: Air emissions accounts: allocation, residence and results
text:
Agreement with the tool

The explicit layer reproduces the I2A function to within 7e-12 kt CO2 eq, with the default and the Tunisian matrices.
Two features of the tool are handled explicitly: the positive maritime gap has no bridging item, and the tool’s own total adds bridging items without their sign.

title: Air emissions accounts: allocation, residence and results
text:
Plausibility: implied emission factors

For each activity, divide CO2 from fuel combustion in the emissions accounts by the fossil energy it uses in the energy accounts.
The result, in tonnes of CO2 per terajoule, should fall near the range of fuels in the inventory: from 57.7 (natural gas) to 76.8 (liquid fuels).

title: Air emissions accounts: allocation, residence and results
text: Implied factors in 2022

title: Air emissions accounts: allocation, residence and results
text:
Reading the factors

Most activities fall inside the band: the two accounts are consistent.
Activities outside the band point to classification differences between the balance and the inventory, for example own use of the energy industries and electricity autoproducers.
These are the places to review with ONEM and ANME.

title: Indicateurs, diffusion et perspectives
text:
Lecture du graphique

Les branches qui utilisent plus d’énergie par dinar émettent aussi plus par dinar.
Les branches au-dessus de la tendance générale émettent pour d’autres raisons que le combustible : ciment (CO2 de procédé), agriculture (méthane), déchets (décharges).

title: Indicateurs, diffusion et perspectives
text:
La place des ménages

Les ménages ont utilisé 34 % de l’utilisation finale d’énergie en 2022 (34 % en 2015).
Ils ont émis 11 % des gaz à effet de serre en 2022 (10 % en 2015).
Leurs émissions viennent des voitures et des logements ; le bois de feu, une grande part de leur énergie, est de la biomasse hors du total de CO2.

Contenu de cette présentation

Comment les catégories de l’inventaire deviennent des branches et des ménages.

title: Comptes des émissions : sources et nomenclatures
text:
Pourquoi des comptes des émissions ?

L’inventaire classe les émissions par procédé : combustion dans les industries énergétiques, transport routier, fermentation entérique, décharges (Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, 2006).
Il ne dit pas quelles unités économiques émettent.
Les comptes réorganisent les mêmes émissions par branche et pour les ménages, comme les comptes nationaux (Eurostat, 2015).
Les émissions peuvent alors être rapprochées de la production, de la valeur ajoutée, de l’emploi et des comptes de l’énergie.

title: Comptes des émissions : sources et nomenclatures
text:
L’inventaire tunisien

Coordonné par l’ANME (énergie, procédés industriels), le ministère de l’Agriculture (agriculture, utilisation des terres) et l’ONAS (déchets) (Besbes, 2026).
Lignes directrices 2006 du GIEC, déclaration dans les tableaux communs de notification (CRT) de la CCNUCC.
En 2022 : 45,8 Mt éq. CO2 hors utilisation des terres ; l’utilisation des terres est un puits net de -10,8 Mt.

title: Comptes des émissions : sources et nomenclatures
text:
Préparation de l’inventaire

Le CO2, le CH4 et le N2O viennent de Data, pondérés par leurs potentiels de réchauffement.
Les gaz fluorés viennent de Summary2, où ils sont en équivalent CO2 par catégorie.
Chaque catégorie reçoit le code le plus détaillé de l’outil I2A dont elle relève.
Le total, utilisation des terres comprise, égale le total net de Summary2, une fois pris en compte un petit écart de N2O.

title: Comptes des émissions : sources et nomenclatures
text:
Deux nomenclatures

Inventaire : quel procédé émet. Transport routier.
Comptes : qui émet. Les ménages qui conduisent leur voiture, les camions de l’agro-alimentaire, les autobus de la branche transport.
Les ménages apparaissent comme consommateurs : leurs voitures et leurs logements. Les ménages producteurs, comme les exploitations familiales, relèvent de leur branche.

Des clés partagées avec les comptes de l’énergie

Le transport routier (1.A.3.b) est réparti entre les branches et les ménages avec la clé routière des comptes de l’énergie.
La combustion du commerce et des services publics (1.A.4.a) est répartie entre les branches de services avec la clé du tertiaire.
Les deux comptes répartissent donc ces secteurs de la même façon.
En 2022, les ménages reçoivent 34 % des émissions du transport routier.

title: Comptes de l’énergie : nomenclatures et répartition
text:
Lecture des clés

Les ménages reçoivent 34 % du carburant routier, le transport 27 %.
Le raffinage et l’électricité sont exclus de la clé routière, car leurs achats de produit 19 sont surtout des entrées de transformation.
Les clés changent chaque année avec les comptes nationaux.
Elles supposent un prix semblable par unité d’énergie pour chaque utilisateur : la meilleure information disponible, mais une hypothèse.

text:
Matrices par défaut et tunisienne

La matrice par défaut de l’outil attribue chaque flux à une section de la CITI.
La matrice tunisienne remplace les lignes des flux couverts par une ligne par branche, avec le facteur de la clé.
Une matrice par année, car les clés changent chaque année.
Les importations, les exportations et les variations de stocks gardent les lignes par défaut.

title: Comptes de l’énergie : nomenclatures et répartition
text:
Ce que fait le convertisseur

Il donne à chaque flux son titre (approvisionnement, transformation, consommation propre, consommation finale).
Il enregistre la production primaire comme une ressource naturelle fournie par l’environnement et utilisée par la branche qui l’extrait.
Il multiplie chaque valeur du bilan par ses facteurs.
Il transforme les sorties de transformation en ressources de produits énergétiques.
Il crée, pour chaque emploi d’énergie, un résidu de même montant qui retourne à l’environnement.

title: Comptes de l’énergie : nomenclatures et répartition
text: De l’origine à l’emploi en 2022

title: Comptes de l’énergie : nomenclatures et répartition
text:
Lecture du diagramme

Le gaz naturel va surtout aux centrales, qui le transforment en électricité.
Les produits pétroliers vont aux ménages, au transport, à l’industrie et à l’agriculture ; du pétrole brut est aussi exporté.
Les biocombustibles, surtout le bois de feu et le charbon de bois, sont utilisés par les ménages.
La transformation apparaît comme un emploi de produits ; sa production réapparaît dans la production nationale.

Chaleur solaire : produite et utilisée par les ménages ? Usages non énergétiques (bitume) : construction ?
L’ONEM pourrait-il répartir la consommation propre de la branche énergie par branche ?
Les achats en valeur sont-ils une clé suffisante pour le transport routier et les services ?

Contenu de cette présentation

Pourquoi les statistiques de l’énergie et des émissions ont besoin de comptes.
Le Système de comptabilité environnementale et économique (SCEE) et ses comptes de l’énergie et des émissions.
Les trois sources tunisiennes qui alimentent les comptes, et l’apport de chacune.

title: Comptes de l’énergie et des émissions
section: Trois systèmes décrivent la même économie
text:
Trois systèmes décrivent la même économie

Les statistiques de l’énergie décrivent les ressources et les emplois des produits énergétiques sur le territoire, par secteur technique. En Tunisie, le bilan énergétique national de l’ONEM.
Les inventaires des gaz à effet de serre décrivent les émissions sur le territoire, par procédé. En Tunisie, l’inventaire coordonné par l’ANME avec le ministère de l’Agriculture et l’ONAS.
Les comptes nationaux décrivent l’économie des unités résidentes, par branche, en valeur. En Tunisie, les tableaux des ressources et des emplois de l’INS.

Les questions des politiques publiques

Quelles branches utilisent le plus d’énergie, et le plus d’énergie par dinar de valeur ajoutée ?
Quelle part de l’énergie des ménages va au transport, à la cuisson ou au chauffage ?
Si l’industrie du ciment croît, de combien les émissions augmentent-elles ?
L’utilisation d’énergie et les émissions croissent-elles plus vite ou moins vite que l’économie ?

Ces questions demandent une énergie et des émissions organisées comme les comptes nationaux.

title: Comptes de l’énergie et des émissions
text:
Le SCEE, une norme internationale

Adopté par la Commission de statistique des Nations unies en 2012 (United Nations et al., 2014).
Un compte satellite du Système de comptabilité nationale : mêmes unités, mêmes nomenclatures, mêmes règles comptables.
Des guides thématiques pour l’énergie (United Nations, 2019) et les émissions atmosphériques ; des manuels de compilation d’Eurostat pour les deux comptes (Eurostat, 2014, 2015).
Les comptes de l’énergie et des émissions atmosphériques sont parmi les comptes du SCEE que les pays compilent le plus souvent.

title: Comptes de l’énergie et des émissions
text:
Trois sortes de flux d’énergie

L’énergie issue des ressources naturelles passe de l’environnement à l’économie : pétrole brut et gaz à l’extraction, soleil, vent, biomasse.
Les produits énergétiques circulent dans l’économie : produits, échangés, transformés, utilisés. Gaz naturel, gasoil, électricité.
Les résidus d’énergie retournent à l’environnement : chaleur de la combustion, électricité perdue sur le réseau, gaz torché au puits.

title: Comptes de l’énergie et des émissions
text:
L’énergie se conserve

L’énergie n’est ni créée ni détruite ; elle change de forme (United Nations, 2019, paragr. 2.14 à 2.21).
Une centrale brûle du gaz : une partie devient de l’électricité (un produit), le reste se perd en chaleur (un résidu).
Un ménage utilise cette électricité : son énergie finit elle aussi en chaleur résiduelle.
Chaque emploi d’énergie a donc un résidu correspondant, et les totaux des tableaux dépassent l’énergie réellement consommée. C’est voulu, et non une erreur.

title: Comptes de l’énergie et des émissions
text:
Territoire et résidence

Le bilan énergétique enregistre ce qui se passe sur le territoire.
Les comptes enregistrent ce que font les unités résidentes, où qu’elles se trouvent (Eurostat, 2014, paragr. 41 à 48).
Une compagnie aérienne tunisienne qui fait le plein à Paris : dans les comptes, pas dans le bilan.
Un navire étranger qui fait le plein à Radès : dans le bilan (soutes), pas dans les comptes.
Un tableau de passage concilie les deux totaux.

title: Comptes de l’énergie et des émissions
text:
Les émissions dans le SCEE

Les émissions sont des flux de résidus vers l’atmosphère (United Nations et al., 2014).
Elles sont enregistrées pour l’unité économique qui émet : les branches, et les ménages en tant que consommateurs (Eurostat, 2015).
Même principe de résidence que les comptes de l’énergie, avec un passage au total de l’inventaire.
L’utilisation des terres, le changement d’affectation des terres et la foresterie restent hors des comptes et figurent dans le passage.

Lecture du graphique

La production nationale comprend des produits secondaires : l’électricité des centrales et les produits de la raffinerie.
La production nationale a baissé sur la période et les importations ont augmenté ; les importations ont dépassé la production nationale en 2019.

section: Les tableaux des ressources et des emplois
text:
Les tableaux des ressources et des emplois

24 produits et autant de branches, en millions de dinars aux prix courants.
Ils donnent aux comptes leurs colonnes : les branches des comptes nationaux.
Leurs achats de carburants et d’électricité fournissent les clés qui répartissent le transport routier et le tertiaire.
Leur production et leur valeur ajoutée transforment l’énergie et les émissions en intensités.
Les ressources égalent les emplois pour chaque produit à 0,08 million de TND près.

L’inventaire des gaz à effet de serre

Un classeur CRT par année ; la feuille Data contient toutes les valeurs déclarées en format long.

Data concorde avec la feuille publiée Summary2 pour chaque catégorie, à une petite exception près (N2O de 1.B.2.b.ii à partir de 2019).
